title: Clinical evidence and regulatory decisions
summary: This edition covers preliminary human data for an experimental optic-neuropathy therapy, a halted Phase 3 program, and a new maintenance indication for a breast-cancer regimen. CAR-T papers and trial registrations lacked independent reporting and are excluded.

stories.headline: Life Biosciences Announces First-in-Human Data from Ongoing Phase 1 Trial Evaluating ER-100 in Optic Neuropathies
stories.dek: The company reported early safety observations and visual-field changes in a three-person Phase 1 cohort; the trial is ongoing and the findings are preliminary.
tldr: Life Biosciences reported first-in-human observations from its ongoing ER-100 Phase 1 study in optic neuropathies.
The company said three participants had completed eight weeks of follow-up and two showed improvement in some visual-field measures.
The small, early cohort does not establish efficacy, and longer follow-up and additional participants are still needed.

body.text: Life Biosciences announced initial human data from its ongoing Phase 1 study of ER-100, an investigational therapy for optic neuropathies including open-angle glaucoma. STAT and TIME also reported on the company’s October 8 presentation. [1][2][3]

The company said three participants had completed eight weeks of follow-up and that the treatment was tolerated during that period. STAT described the update as an early safety readout; TIME reported that two participants showed changes in portions of their visual fields. [1][2][3]

ER-100 is being tested in a Phase 1 trial, whose primary purpose is to assess safety and tolerability. The reports describe a very small initial group and preliminary observations, not a controlled demonstration that the therapy improves vision. [1][2][3]

The study remains ongoing, and the cited coverage does not provide a full peer-reviewed dataset or establish how durable the reported changes may be. Safety over longer follow-up, results in a larger group, and whether later studies confirm a clinical benefit remain open. [1][2]

stories.whyItMatters: The update is an early clinical milestone for partial epigenetic reprogramming in people, but the size and stage of the study sharply limit what can be concluded about benefit.
stories.editorNote: TODO-review: Verify the detailed visual-field endpoints against the conference presentation before expanding this summary. Company-reported preliminary data; no efficacy conclusion.

stories.headline: argenx Provides Update on Phase 3 UNITY Study of Efgartigimod SC in Sjögren's Disease
stories.dek: An independent monitoring committee recommended stopping the study for futility after an interim analysis found it unlikely to meet its primary endpoint.
tldr: argenx said it will discontinue the Phase 3 UNITY study of subcutaneous efgartigimod in adults with moderate-to-severe Sjögren's disease.
The company said an independent monitoring committee recommended stopping for futility because the trial was unlikely to meet its primary endpoint.
The company reported no new safety signals; a separate Phase 2 celiac-disease result was positive but does not reverse the UNITY outcome.

body.text: argenx said it will discontinue UNITY, a Phase 3 study testing subcutaneous efgartigimod in adults with moderate-to-severe Sjögren’s disease. BioPharma Dive and Investing.com also reported the halt and the company’s explanation. [1][2][3]

The company said an independent data monitoring committee recommended stopping the trial for futility after an interim analysis. The committee concluded that the study was unlikely to meet its primary endpoint; the company did not present the interim efficacy dataset in the cited announcement. [1][2]

argenx said safety was consistent with the established profile of efgartigimod and that no new safety signals were identified. BioPharma Dive reported that a separate Phase 2 study of FB102 in celiac disease met its primary endpoint, a distinct program from UNITY. [1][2]

The decision removes this Phase 3 Sjögren’s study from the program, but the announcement does not establish why the interim result missed the endpoint or how it affects other efgartigimod indications. Further detail on the interim analysis and the company’s broader development plans remains limited. [1][2][3]

stories.whyItMatters: The stop is a late-stage clinical setback for an attempted expansion of an existing autoimmune therapy; the separate celiac result belongs to another drug program and should not be conflated with it.
stories.editorNote: The futility determination is attributed to the independent monitoring committee and company release. No investment or treatment advice.

stories.headline: Pfizer’s TUKYSA Regimen Receives FDA Approval as Front-Line Maintenance Treatment for HER2+ Metastatic Breast Cancer
stories.dek: The FDA cleared tucatinib with trastuzumab and pertuzumab for maintenance after induction treatment in adults with unresectable locally advanced or metastatic HER2-positive disease.
tldr: The FDA approved tucatinib with trastuzumab and pertuzumab for maintenance treatment of certain adults with HER2-positive advanced breast cancer.
The decision followed induction treatment and was supported by the randomized HER2CLIMB-05 study of 654 patients.
The FDA reported median progression-free survival of 24.9 months with tucatinib versus 16.3 months with placebo; overall survival data remain immature.

body.text: The FDA approved tucatinib with trastuzumab and pertuzumab as maintenance treatment for adults with unresectable locally advanced or metastatic HER2-positive breast cancer after induction treatment. Pfizer announced the approval on October 7. [1][2]

The FDA said efficacy was evaluated in HER2CLIMB-05, a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study involving 654 adults who had no disease progression after four to eight cycles of induction treatment. Patients received tucatinib or placebo alongside trastuzumab and pertuzumab. [1]

The FDA reported median investigator-assessed progression-free survival of 24.9 months in the tucatinib group and 16.3 months in the placebo group. Pfizer’s announcement reported the same trial result and characterized the regimen as a chemotherapy-free maintenance option. [1][2]

The FDA noted that overall survival data were immature at the analysis and that the safety profile was consistent with known risks of the medicines. The approval applies to the specified population and treatment sequence; it does not establish outcomes for patients outside those criteria. [1]

stories.whyItMatters: The decision moves a three-drug regimen into a first-line maintenance setting for a defined HER2-positive population, with the FDA’s review tied to a randomized trial and a specified treatment sequence.
stories.editorNote: Regulatory reporting only. The label and full prescribing information govern the approved population and safety information.
